title: Cross-border transmission can reach commercial operation before household affordability is visible
source_unit: NYSERDA and New York State announcement of commercial operation of the Champlain Hudson Power Express transmission project
geography: Quebec, Canada; New York State; New York City Zone J

observations.period: June 16, 2026 announcement; commercial operation reported May 13, 2026

physical_delivery.unit: terawatt-hours of clean energy expected per year delivered into the New York metro area

system_reach.unit: percent of New York City's energy needs the project is expected to meet

cross_border_dependency.value: Hydro-Québec power delivered through a 339-mile transmission line into NYISO Zone J

public_claims.value: 37 million metric tons of carbon emissions expected to be reduced through 2040 and more than 1,400 construction and operations jobs supported
public_claims.unit: reported projected public and labor effects

household_bill_effect_and_local_acceptan.unit: missing customer-level bill, affordability, reliability, burden, and durable acceptance outcome

observations.method: Official NYSERDA/New York State project announcement and NYSERDA Tier Four program page; commercial operation, delivered-energy route, cross-border dependency, and projected public effects are coded separately from realized household bills, rate allocation, reliability, and acceptance.
observations.uncertainty: The announcement reports commercial operation and expected annual delivery, but does not provide customer-level bill changes, rate-class allocation, actual monthly delivery series, reliability outcomes, project cost incidence, or later public acceptance. The public-health and emissions figures are projections or modeled effects rather than person-level outcomes.
observations.subgroup: New York City and New York State electricity customers, communities along the route, Hydro-Québec and New York system operators, construction and operations workers, and communities described as disadvantaged; subgroup-level realized effects are not reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: A cross-border project can create real operating capacity and reduce emissions while its costs, benefits, and reliability effects are distributed unevenly. Commercial operation does not show that a household received cheaper or more reliable service, or that host communities accepted the project over time.

observations.period: July 3-4, 2026; heat-event operation and early reliability friction

denominator.unit: NYISO daily electricity-import and CHPE operational episode

canadian_imports.unit: gigawatt-hours imported from Canada by NYISO on July 3, 2026

nyiso_import_share.unit: percent of NYISO electricity demand supplied by Canadian imports on July 3

chpe_utilization.unit: megawatts of CHPE capacity fully utilized on July 3

reliability_friction.value: EIA reported that an outage occurred in June and that CHPE was taken offline again on July 4 for further repairs

mechanism.value: Commercial operation converted infrastructure promise into observable grid use during heat stress, while the early outage-and-repair episode shows that operation is a sequence of availability and interruption rather than a binary milestone

observations.method: U.S. Energy Information Administration analysis using NYISO hourly electric-grid data and official project context.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not isolate CHPE's causal effect on wholesale prices, retail bills, emissions, or reliability; the import total includes Canadian flows beyond CHPE, and the outage account does not provide duration, repair cost, or customer-level incidence.
observations.subgroup: NYISO electricity users, New York City Zone J, Hydro-Québec, NYISO operators, and communities affected by the transmission system; household outcomes are not individually observed.
observations.counterinterpretation: High utilization during a heat event can show valuable capacity while an early outage can be routine commissioning friction; neither alone establishes durable reliability or affordability.

denominator.unit: named CHPE operator public status page

operator_status.value: The project operator's public site describes CHPE as fully operational after commissioning and says the state contract began June 1, 2026

availability_verification.value: not independently observed in this record
availability_verification.unit: missing post-repair hourly availability, outage duration, and dispatch series

reliability_context.value: A contemporaneous reliability record still treats demonstration of planned CHPE capability as relevant to New York City reliability needs

mechanism.value: Recovery claims and system-level reliability qualification are separate stages: an operator can report restored operation while independent evidence of sustained availability and customer effect remains necessary

observations.method: Operator public status page cross-read with public NYISO/utility reliability reporting; operator claim is preserved separately from independent operational verification.
observations.uncertainty: The operator page is not an independent availability dataset and does not report outage duration, dispatch, maintenance, delivered energy, price effect, or customer incidence; the reliability-planning condition is not a post-repair performance measure.
observations.subgroup: New York City electricity users, NYISO and utility reliability planners, Hydro-Québec, CHPE operator, and route communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: The operator's fully-operational statement may accurately describe restored commercial status even if short interruptions or capacity constraints remain; reliability planning can also remain conservative after a project enters service.

observations.period: 2026-2027 capability-year planning; CHPE-in versus CHPE-out market case

denominator.unit: planning cases for New York's 2026-2027 locational capacity requirements

nyc_lcr_chpe_in.unit: percent New York City locational capacity requirement in the CHPE-in case

nyc_lcr_chpe_out.unit: percent New York City locational capacity requirement in the CHPE-out case

market_governance.value: The capacity framework explicitly distinguishes whether CHPE is available for the planning case, showing that project status enters resource-adequacy and market-governance calculations

incidence_boundary.value: The planning-case difference does not identify a retail bill change, customer savings, outage reduction, or equal benefit distribution

mechanism.value: Infrastructure realization can alter formal market requirements before its costs and benefits are traceable to households or local communities

observations.method: New York State Association of Counties market update summarizing New York State Reliability Council and NYISO 2026-2027 locational-capacity planning cases.
observations.uncertainty: The planning cases are scenario inputs and do not measure realized CHPE availability, market-clearing prices, retail bills, reliability outcomes, or customer incidence; the summary is not the underlying NYISO calculation file.
observations.subgroup: NYISO Zone J load-serving entities, capacity-market participants, New York electricity customers, and planners using CHPE-in/CHPE-out reliability cases.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different planning cases can reflect methodology and timing assumptions rather than an observed causal effect of CHPE on market prices or reliability.

observations.period: August 2026 announcement; 2027 Tier 4 voluntary REC sales route

denominator.unit: NYSERDA public voluntary-sale administrative route for Tier 4 RECs associated with CHPE delivery

verified_product.value: A Tier 4 REC represents one megawatt-hour of eligible renewable energy generated and delivered into NYISO Zone J, with generation, delivery, and attributes verified and tracked by New York State

sale_and_payment_timing.value: NYSERDA describes a 14-day sale window, pro-rata allocation if demand exceeds supply, invoice within seven business days, and payment due within 30 calendar days

realized_transaction_and_incidence.unit: missing buyer-level allocation, completed payment, electricity bill effect, retail customer receipt, and route-community outcome

observations.method: Bounded extraction from NYSERDA's official Tier 4 voluntary-sales page; administrative product verification and payment timing are kept separate from a completed sale or downstream customer benefit.
observations.uncertainty: The page states the sales mechanism and timing but does not disclose a completed 2027 transaction, purchaser allocation, payment receipt, REC price in this record, retail bill effect, or local acceptance.
observations.subgroup: NYSERDA, Hydro-Québec/CHPE contract participants, voluntary REC buyers, load-serving entities, New York electricity customers, and route communities; no buyer- or customer-level outcome sample is supplied.
observations.counterinterpretation: A precise administrative sales route can make payment governance auditable while leaving actual delivery, payment completion, and downstream affordability unobserved.

observations.period: September 30, 2026 preschedule; October 12-16 planned interruption and October 17-30 restoration

scheduled_transfer_capacity.value: 1,250 MW scheduled and available in the public preschedule through October 11, 0 MW from October 12 through October 16, and 1,250 MW again from October 17 through October 30

operating_stage.value: The public planning snapshot records a second dated interruption/recovery window after the earlier summer outage and operator-reported restoration

customer_incidence.unit: missing dispatch, outage duration, retail bill, reliability, customer-class, and route-community effect

observations.method: Structured extraction from the NYISO public Long Term ATC/TTC preschedule page, retaining the HQ-CHPE daily interface values as a planning/availability record rather than treating them as metered delivery.
observations.uncertainty: The preschedule reports transfer capability and planned interface status, not actual dispatch, physical delivery, outage cause, customer interruption, retail price, bill effect, or compensation. The page was observed through the public indexed HTML view; a direct retrieval recheck returned 404, so the source remains a bounded public-record observation rather than a preserved downloadable archive.
observations.subgroup: NYISO operators, Hydro-Québec/CHPE, New York load-serving entities, Zone J electricity users, and route communities; no customer-level outcome is supplied.
observations.counterinterpretation: A zero prescheduled interface value can reflect planned maintenance, market scheduling, or a data-window convention rather than a customer outage; restoration of scheduled capability does not prove realized delivery or benefit.

observations.period: September 2, 2026 completed 2027-vintage voluntary REC sale; payment and retirement stages remain open

denominator.unit: NYSERDA voluntary Tier 4 REC sale associated with CHPE delivery

presale_revenue.unit: US dollars in reported presale revenue

avoided_ratepayer_cost_claim.unit: approximately US dollars in reported avoided ratepayer costs

downstream_incidence.unit: missing completed payment, REC retirement, buyer pass-through, household credit, retail bill, and route-community outcome

mechanism.value: A verified infrastructure attribute can produce a dated program-level sale and avoided-cost claim without establishing equal household benefit or retail pass-through

observations.method: Structured extraction from NYSERDA's official 2027 Tier 4 voluntary-sales summary; the reported sale, revenue, and avoided-cost claim are retained separately from completed payment, retirement, and customer incidence.
observations.uncertainty: The official summary reports aggregate offer, sale, price, revenue, and avoided-cost figures but does not identify buyer-level allocation, completed payment, REC retirement, retail bill posting, household receipt, or route-community acceptance. The avoided-cost figure is a program-level claim, not an equal per-household credit.
observations.subgroup: NYSERDA, CHPE/Hydro-Québec contract participants, voluntary REC buyers, load-serving entities, New York electricity customers, ratepayers, and route communities; no linked household or buyer outcome sample is supplied.
observations.counterinterpretation: A completed aggregate REC sale can provide a real administrative and financial endpoint while still leaving payment timing, downstream allocation, affordability, and legitimacy unresolved.

observations.period: June-September 2026 first-summer operating profile; analysis published September 29, 2026

denominator.unit: named CHPE transmission project observed across five-minute operating intervals and hot-day Zone J market conditions

zero_output_intervals.unit: percent of five-minute intervals during June-August reported at zero output

average_running_output.unit: megawatts average running output against 1,250 MW rating

forced_outage_window.unit: full operational days removed by the cable-fault period beginning July 4

hot_day_day_ahead_spread.value: $17/MW-day when CHPE ran versus $85/MW-day when it did not on 85-90F days
hot_day_day_ahead_spread.unit: reported Zone J day-ahead four-hour spread premium

household_incidence.unit: missing retail bill, rate-class allocation, customer reliability, outage compensation, and route-community acceptance

mechanism.value: Infrastructure availability can be intermittent yet conditionally associated with a wholesale spread difference; neither pattern alone establishes causal retail savings or household reliability protection

observations.method: Structured extraction from Modo Energy's first-summer CHPE analysis using five-minute operating and market data; secondary market interpretation is retained separately from an independent causal or household-bill evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: The source is a secondary market-data analysis and does not provide an independently reproduced counterfactual, retail bill linkage, rate-class allocation, outage-service effect, repair cost, compensation, or route-community outcome. Conditional spread differences may reflect operating selection and do not establish causality.
observations.subgroup: CHPE and NYISO operators, Zone J market participants, New York electricity customers, rate classes, and route communities; no customer-level outcome sample is supplied.
observations.counterinterpretation: A 13% first-summer capacity factor and a 20-day fault-related removal can coexist with useful hot-day operation; observed wholesale spread differences do not by themselves prove project success or failure for households.

denominator.unit: NYISO daily capacity-report snapshot containing the HQ-CHPE import schedule

chpe_import_limit.unit: megawatts listed as the CHPE import limit

nyca_capacity_margin.unit: megawatts reported NYCA capacity margin in the snapshot

customer_incidence.unit: missing retail customer, bill, avoided interruption, facility payment, and household/service outcome

mechanism.value: An independent system-operator snapshot can confirm that a named cross-border import enters daily capacity accounting without proving realized delivery, customer reliability, or affordability

observations.method: Structured extraction from NYISO's official daily capacity report; the snapshot is retained as an operational/accounting observation rather than a metered-delivery or customer-benefit measure.
observations.uncertainty: A single daily report cannot establish sustained availability, dispatch, market-clearing price, avoided outage, retail bill effect, payment incidence, or route-community response. The scheduled value is not equivalent to delivered energy.
observations.subgroup: NYISO operators, CHPE/Hydro-Québec, New York load-serving entities, Zone J electricity users, and route communities; no customer-level outcome is supplied.
observations.counterinterpretation: A fully scheduled import can coexist with later outage, congestion, price, or customer-service problems; the snapshot confirms system accounting, not realized household benefit.

related_sources.claim: New York load-serving entities have a 2026 obligation tied to Tier 4 renewable energy certificates delivered through the project into NYISO Zone J.
related_sources.access_boundary: The obligation and delivered-energy accounting route do not establish a household bill change or individual receipt.

related_sources.claim: NYSERDA describes an hourly verification chain: eligible generation, scheduling, and delivery into NYISO Zone J must match before a Tier 4 REC is minted and payment is issued to Hydro-Québec.
related_sources.access_boundary: This establishes an administrative delivery-and-payment control for the project contract, not a retail bill change, customer-level receipt, affordability result, or route-community acceptance.

related_sources.claim: NYSERDA's public Tier 4 voluntary-sales route describes verified CHPE-associated REC units, a 14-day sale window, pro-rata allocation, seven-business-day invoicing, and payment due within 30 calendar days.
related_sources.access_boundary: The public process establishes an administrative payment route, not a completed transaction, buyer-level receipt, retail bill effect, or household affordability result.

related_sources.claim: NYISO's September 30 public preschedule lists the HQ-CHPE interface at 1,250 MW through October 11, 0 MW from October 12 through October 16, and 1,250 MW again from October 17 through October 30.
related_sources.access_boundary: The preschedule is a transmission-capability/planning record; it does not establish actual dispatch, customer interruption, retail bill effect, or route-community response, and direct retrieval was unavailable at recheck.

boundary: This record establishes a cross-border infrastructure project reaching commercial operation and a reported route for clean electricity delivery into New York. It does not establish realized household affordability, customer-class allocation, reliability improvement, host-community acceptance, or durable geopolitical leverage. It is an infrastructure and state-dependence realization case, not a household benefit estimate.
